title: A 94.8nW Battery-Free Intelligent Silicon Platform Enabling Distributed, Adaptive, and Event-Driven Multimodal Sensing at the Edge
problem: Ultra-low-power (ULP) edge sensors with ML must operate from 100nW harvested energy while supporting distributed, multimodal sensing and model adaptation. Current systems suffer from isolated monomodal operation, limited task complexity, and high power overhead of NN accelerators that prevent network expansion.
method: A 94.8nW battery-free platform integrates adaptive event-driven multimodal sensing with an ultra-low-power NN accelerator. The design enables model adaptation for handling data distribution shifts while supporting collaborative sensing across distributed sensor nodes through efficient power management.

title: Lincoln: Real-Time 50~100B LLM Inference on Consumer Devices with LPDDR-Interfaced, Compute-Enabled Flash Memory
problem: Consumer devices cannot run large 50-100B LLM models in real time because: (1) Flash storage has insufficient internal read bandwidth for per-iteration weight loading, and (2) the conventional Flash interface (NVMe/UFS) offers far lower transmission bandwidth to the NPU than DRAM interfaces, making both the prefill and decode phases severely bandwidth-limited.
method: Lincoln is a device-architecture co-design with two complementary solutions for the two LLM phases. For the compute-intensive prefill phase, Flash devices use the existing high-speed LPDDR interface (normally used for DRAM) to transmit weights to the NPU at much higher bandwidth than conventional Flash interfaces, while maintaining cost/area efficiency. For the memory-intensive decode phase, hybrid-bonding-based near-Flash computing performs matrix-vector operations directly on Flash dies to exploit the full internal Flash bandwidth without transmission bottlenecks, coupled with speculative decoding to further reduce latency. On the device level, Flash internal bandwidth is increased by improving array shrinking methods (lower read latency, more parallel Flash planes per die), leveraging 3D hybrid bonding already in consumer Flash products.

title: DS-TPU: Dynamical System for on-Device Lifelong Graph Learning with Nonlinear Node Interaction
problem: Electronic Dynamical System (DS) hardware achieves orders-of-magnitude speed and energy improvements over GNNs for graph inference via natural annealing, but it (1) lacks native on-device training support—forcing reliance on slower conventional hardware for model updates—and (2) restricts node interactions to linear functions, limiting expressiveness and training accuracy.
method: DS-TPU introduces two algorithmic-architectural co-design innovations. First, an on-device lifelong learning mechanism uses feedback electric current as a native loss signal in response to observed training data, enabling electron-speed model parameter refinement directly on the DS chip without off-chip software. Second, nonlinear DS node interactions are constructed from Chebyshev polynomial expansions, making the DS hardware compatible with the richer relational structure in graph data while remaining implementable in analog hardware. The DS-TPU architecture is evaluated at a 5-Watt power envelope on six real-world graph learning benchmarks.

title: OASIS: Object-Aware Page Management for Multi-GPU Systems
problem: Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) in multi-GPU systems applies a single, application-object-agnostic page placement and migration policy to all data, failing to account for the fact that different data objects and different execution phases of the same object benefit from different page management strategies.
method: OASIS dynamically identifies application object access patterns at runtime by monitoring page-access counters and tracking object-level access behaviors across execution phases. Based on the detected patterns, it proactively assigns one of several page management policies—on-touch migration, access-counter-based migration, or duplication—to each object on a per-phase basis. The policy decision logic runs in software/hardware coordination and uses lightweight profiling to adapt to phase changes without manual programmer annotation.

title: VR-Pipe: Streamlining Hardware Graphics Pipeline for Volume Rendering
problem: Radiance field rendering methods (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting) are evaluated only on software-based shader pipelines, leaving performance on fixed-function GPU hardware graphics units unexplored and suboptimal for volume rendering workloads.
method: VR-Pipe integrates two hardware innovations into the fixed-function GPU graphics pipeline: (1) native early termination support by repurposing existing special-purpose hardware (e.g., depth test units) to terminate ray marching when accumulated opacity saturates; (2) multi-granular tile binning with quad merging, which opportunistically blends fragments in programmable shader cores before passing them to fixed-function blending units, reducing blending bottlenecks. The design targets the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline as a concrete instantiation.

title: Bridging FPGA and GPU over PCIe: A Low-Latency Communication Path using AVX-512
problem: Inter-accelerator communication bottlenecks; high latency and complexity in GPU-FPGA bridging
method: Programmed I/O using AVX-512 instructions for PCIe communication; GPU peer-to-peer memory mapping

title: Optimizing Microgrid Composition for Sustainable Data Centers
problem: Data centers increasingly use colocated microgrids with renewable energy and storage, but lack tools to assess how microgrid sizing and composition affect long-term sustainability and power reliability. Existing research focuses on operational vs embodied carbon tradeoffs but not on microgrid design optimization.
method: Extend Vessim (computing/energy co-simulator) with detailed renewable energy generation models from NREL's System Advisor Model (SAM). Implement multi-horizon black-box optimization to explore efficient microgrid compositions. Simulate workload-renewable-storage interaction capturing both operational and embodied emissions.

title: Architecting Tensor Core-Based Reductions for Irregular Molecular Docking Kernels
problem: Tensor Cores are optimized for dense matrix operations but molecular docking has irregular computation patterns; their adoption in such HPC applications remains limited.
method: Twofold strategy: (1) accelerate sum reduction operations using Tensor Cores, (2) apply numerical error correction (EC) techniques to maintain accuracy. CUDA implementation on A100, H100, B200.

title: 27.3 A Sub-1V 14b 5.8nW/Hz BW/Power-Scalable CT Sensor Interface with a Frequency-Controlled Current Source Achieving a 225× Scalable Range
problem: Sensor interfaces for weak signals (tens of mV: shunt current sensors, biomedical) require low noise and scalable bandwidth/power for different IoT applications; discrete-time ADCs suffer from kT/C noise, while continuous-time front-ends consume fixed power.
method: Continuous-time (CT) sensor interface using frequency-controlled current source that enables scalable bandwidth and power dissipation across a 225× range. CT front-stage suppresses kT/C sampling noise while frequency tuning allows bandwidth-power trade-offs.

title: A Nested Krylov Method Using Half-Precision Arithmetic
problem: Leveraging half-precision (fp16) arithmetic in iterative sparse linear solvers is challenging despite the bandwidth and performance benefits it offers.
method: Nested Krylov approach integrating FGMRES and Richardson methods in deeply nested structure with progressive precision reduction (double → fp16). Low-precision inner solvers perform limited iterations but execute frequently; nested structure ensures convergence.

title: Optimizing Datalog for the GPU
problem: Modern Datalog engines designed for CPUs cannot efficiently exploit GPU parallelism due to the relational algebra operations over sparse, recursively updated fact sets that do not map well to dense GPU data structures. Existing GPU join implementations also carry high memory overhead for recursive workloads like points-to analysis.
method: GPUlog implements a Datalog engine backend on data center GPUs by introducing the Hash-Indexed Sorted Array (HISA), a novel range-indexed data structure that combines incremental range indexing (for efficient semi-naive evaluation of recursive Datalog) with dense array operations amenable to GPU throughput. Iterated relational algebra kernels (join, union, difference) are implemented over HISA, enabling GPU-native semi-naive evaluation with favorable memory footprint compared to GPU hash-join baselines.

title: HoBBy: Hardening Unbalanced Branches against Control Flow Attacks on Intel SGX and AMD SEV
problem: Control flow attacks (e.g., spectre, side-channel exploits) on Intel SGX and AMD SEV exploit timing differences between balanced and unbalanced branches in secret-dependent code, bypassing source-level defenses that operate only at instruction granularity.
method: Compiler-based technique that identifies unbalanced instructions in secret-dependent branches via single-step analysis, then applies instruction-level transformations: shadowing (duplicate ops), cogging (interleave), and spiraling (permute) to make parallel control flows indistinguishable to attackers.

title: Agentic AI vs ML-based Autotuning: A Comparative Study for Loop Reordering Optimization
problem: Traditional ML-based autotuning approaches for HPC code optimization require expensive compile-run evaluations and lack adaptability for large applications. Emerging Agentic AI systems offer alternative optimization paradigms with unclear practical advantages.
method: Comparative analysis between traditional ML autotuner and novel LoopGen-AI agent system using three LLMs (GPT-4.1, Claude 4.0, Gemini 2.5). Evaluation on loop-level optimization (loop reordering). Prompt engineering with Persona + Context Manager patterns. Analysis of convergence, sample efficiency, and decision quality.

title: 29.2 A 0.021μm2 High-Density SRAM in Intel-18A-RibbonFET Technology with PowerVia-Backside Power Delivery
problem: Advancing to sub-2nm nodes requires higher density and lower V_MIN (minimum operating voltage) to maintain power efficiency; FinFET bitcell scaling limits are reached; traditional frontend power distribution uses valuable signal routing tracks.
method: 6T SRAM bitcell in Intel 18A RibbonFET technology with flexible transistor-width tuning. PowerVia provides low-resistance backside power rails reducing power droop. Bitcell layout co-optimized with peripheral circuit compaction to maximize density while maintaining V_MIN without read/write assist.

title: On the integration of lightweight tasks with MPI using the C++26 std::execution 'Senders' API
problem: Integrating asynchronous MPI messaging with tasking runtimes requires careful handling of request polling and completion dispatching. Existing approaches lack clean abstractions for this integration.
method: Implement Senders API in pika tasking runtime. Wrap asynchronous MPI calls as execution nodes in computation graph. Experiment with different polling and completion dispatching strategies.

title: Hot ChipsKeynote
problem: Keynote presentation; no specific technical problem addressed.
method: Keynote address covering emerging trends and research opportunities.
